environment.directories: lab: http://198.18.0.1:8080/; realworld and startup: http://213.163.75.157:56050/ (temporary, on p2p-relay1); relay step: 127.0.0.1 on the Hetzner machine
environment.paths: As in campaigns 1 and 2. Lab: every access link 10 ms each way, relay link 10 ms each way (direct RTT ~40 ms, relayed ~80 ms); lossy1 50 ms + 1 % loss each way. Hetzner <-> i3D host: per flow either ~34 ms or ~37.5 ms RTT (the two route clusters of every campaign); lab nodes with uplink=real reach the real relay through the i3D host's hairpin NAT in < 1 ms.
environment.bench_settings: defaults of c270dde: latency 12 s (was 10 s) at 200 ms, 64 B, packet loss counted from when the selected path has been stable for max(1 s, 3 x min RTT) (peer.latency.loss); upload and download 10 MB each, stopped at 8 s (an upload is reset there and the listener reports what arrived; the bench waits for that count max(3 s, the upload's duration, 3 smoothed RTTs), at most 30 s; campaign 2: 3 s); concurrency 8 streams of echo requests, 8 MB, 256 KiB each or smaller on a slow link (sized so that each stream can finish about four in 8 s at the slower of the measured upload/download throughput, concurrency.sized_for_mbps), requests still running at 8 s are cut off; relay transfers capped at 4 MB; relay_fallback_failed only if nothing got through the relay-only connection (relay_compare.reachable), else relay_fallback_degraded; timeout 10 s; --compare-relay and --idle 60s where listed. The relay group uses --relay-only on both sides; the parallel relay runs skip the concurrency phase.
environment.method: Same scenarios (scenarios.jsonl identical to campaign 2's), run counts and order as campaigns 1 and 2 (harness/campaign/campaign3.sh = campaign2.sh with a new name, output directory and comparison): every run starts fresh processes (new iroh keys and ports; bench uses a temporary identity); 3 runs per scenario, rounds interleaved; parallel relay runs: 2 rounds of 2 and of 4 benches. Scenario side a = the bench (client, dialer), b = the listen node. Verdicts classified by summarize.py, which judges each campaign by the rules of its own bench (packet_loss: 2 % of the whole connection in campaign 1, 0.5 % of >= 50 latency-phase packets in campaign 2, the same from when the path had settled now); re-run on the raw data of campaigns 1 and 2 it reproduces their classification exactly. Extra: 10 more lab-netem-pr runs (same nodes and arguments, --compare-relay) after the campaign, in debug/lossy-extra (not in summary.json), for the loss detection rate, the settle window, the relay fallback and the request sizing on the lossy link.
environment.sides: a = the node running `golem-p2p bench` (it dials), b = the node running `golem-p2p listen`

observations.title: No packet_loss false positives any more: 0 of 90 clean-link peer runs (campaign 2: 21)
observations.detail: Every peer run reported peer.latency.loss (never null): counted from 0 ms in the 56 runs that were direct from the first packet or relay-only, and from ~1.24 s (lab and real world alike) in the 34 runs whose hole punching finished during the latency phase. The settled windows held 112-145 packets and lost none. 20 of those 90 runs lost 1-5 packets in the whole latency phase (peer.latency.quic, campaign 2's input), all in the hole-punched runs: by campaign 2's rule they would have been false positives again, so the settle window removes exactly that artefact. No run listed packet_loss as unknown.

observations.title: Lossy link: loss detected in 11 of 13 runs, the count always settled
observations.detail: lab-netem-pr (1 % loss each way): packet_loss hint in 2 of 3 campaign runs and 9 of 10 extra runs (debug/lossy-extra), 11/13. latency.loss was never null: counting started 1.1-2.7 s into the phase (hole punching took 0.7-1.7 s on this link), windows of 103-124 packets, 1-3 lost where detected. The two misses lost 0 of 115 and 0 of 119 packets; at 1 % random loss about 30 % of such windows show no loss, so this is the measurement's resolution, not a bug (campaign 2: 2/3 with a whole-phase count that also included hole-punching artefacts).

observations.title: Relay fallback on the lossy link: healthy in 13 of 13 runs (campaign 2: failed in 2 of 3)
observations.detail: relay_compare ok and reachable in all 3 campaign runs and all 10 extra runs; no relay_fallback_failed and no relay_fallback_degraded. The relayed uploads stopped at 8 s were counted 10.8-15.3 s after their start, i.e. 2.8-7.3 s after the stop (campaign 2 gave up after 3 s); the wait is now at least as long as the upload ran (8 s), so all counts arrived. The relayed path gave 0.7-1.6 Mbps up (13 Mbps in one size-limited run) and 0.8-1.4 Mbps down. relay_compare takes 25-36 s on this link.

observations.title: Concurrency on the lossy link measures again in 11 of 13 runs, but sizing from a lucky transfer can still leave it empty
observations.detail: Requests sized for 1.0-6.1 Mbps (29-186 KiB instead of 256 KiB): 0.6-2.5 Mbps in 3/3 campaign runs and 8/10 extra runs (campaign 2: no throughput in 3/3, campaign 1: 1/3). In 2 extra runs (debug/lossy-extra run8 and run10) the requests were sized for 4.7 and 6.7 Mbps (the slower of upload/download, or the download alone when the upload failed) and none of the 8 parallel 142-204 KiB echo requests finished in 8 s (throughput null, phase ok). On this link single transfers swing between ~1 and ~37 Mbps from run to run (a loss early in slow start or not), while the steady state at 1 % loss and 120 ms RTT is ~1-2 Mbps, so the measured figure can overestimate the link by more than the 4x margin. Sizing for a lower figure (e.g. a quarter of the slower transfer again, or the minimum also over the latency-phase RTT/loss) or counting the bytes of unfinished requests would close the gap.

observations.title: New bug: an upload that finishes just before the time limit can fail with 'closed stream'
observations.detail: debug/lossy-extra run10: the listener received all 10,000,000 bytes after 7.9 s (its sink event), but the bench's upload failed at exactly 8.0 s with 'read error: closed stream: closed stream' (error_kind transfer), so the run got a transfer_failed issue, status degraded and exit 5, a misleading verdict for a working upload. In probe::upload, once everything is written the read of the listener's count runs under the same 8 s deadline (timeout_at); when the count is still in flight then, the read is cancelled, the code takes the 'stopped by time' branch, resets the already finished send stream and reads the recv stream a second time, which fails with ClosedStream. Fix: after a complete write, wait for the count with count_wait instead of the transfer deadline (and never re-read a stream whose read_to_end was cancelled). Seen once in 13 lossy runs, never in the 111 campaign runs (on fast paths uploads end well before 8 s).

observations.title: Concurrency throughput on fast paths is quantized by the 200 ms --interval tick (all campaigns)
observations.detail: The concurrency phase ends only when its loaded-RTT loop notices that the workers are done, at its next 200 ms tick (or when its small request in flight is cut off), and duration_ms is taken after that. So the phase lasts ~203, 224, 240, 403 or 803 ms and 7.5 MiB give 309, 280, 262, 156 or 78 Mbps (every lab direct run: 156 Mbps = 7.5 MiB / 403 ms; relay-only 78 Mbps); the workers themselves may have finished up to 200 ms earlier. The compare flags rw-easy-to-open 262 -> 156 and rw-open-to-easy 156 -> 280 Mbps are one tick more or less, not a change. Taking the elapsed time when the workers finish (or selecting on the done flag in the tick wait) would fix it; slow links (seconds) are hardly affected.

observations.title: Run durations: +2 s per peer run (the 12 s latency phase), lossy runs unchanged
observations.detail: Every clean peer run takes 2.0 s longer (e.g. lab 12.6 -> 14.6 s, with --compare-relay 20.3 -> 22.3 s, --idle 60s 72.7 -> 74.7 s, real world 11.4-17.9 -> 13.4-20.0 s). lab-netem-pr: 58-70.5 s (campaign 2: 61-69 s), extra runs 64-72 s: the longer count wait (upload phase up to 8.1 s, relayed upload up to 15.3 s) is offset by fewer failed transfers; relay_compare 25-36 s. Local-only startup runs are unchanged (0.2-3.4 s). The whole campaign took 40 min (campaign 2: 37 min).

observations.title: Outcomes, RTT and throughput unchanged
observations.detail: All 35 scenarios keep their direct/relay outcome; final paths 51 direct / 42 relay / 0 failed in the 93 peer runs, no connection lost, QUIC counters in all 93 (as in campaign 2). Lab RTT (40.4 ms direct, 80.6 ms relayed), throughput (122-124 / 35 Mbps), bind and connect times match campaign 2 within noise. Real-world RTT and throughput moved with the two route clusters (~34 / ~37.5 ms). Two real-world runs at 23:33-23:34 UTC (rw-udp-blocked-to-ufw run 1 via the relay, rw-easy-to-open run 1 direct, both Hetzner -> lab VM) got 8.8 and 13.8 Mbps down: a short slowdown on the internet path, not the code. Whole-connection loss of the rw-open-to-* runs rose to 4.6-4.9 % (congestion losses of the bulk phases, not judged).

observations.title: Verdicts: 110 runs right, 1 misleading, 0 wrong (campaign 2: 88 / 23 / 0)
observations.detail: All 21 packet_loss_unshaped and both relay_fallback_failed_but_works runs of campaign 2 are gone. The one misleading run is lab-netem-pr run 3: 1 % loss on the link, but 0 of the 115 packets in the settled window were lost, so no hint (sampling). Not counted (debug runs): the misleading transfer_failed of debug/lossy-extra run10 (the upload race above).

observations.title: The real relay is not a bottleneck at the tested load (unchanged)
observations.detail: Relay-only Hetzner -> p2p-relay1 -> Hetzner: 40.5 Mbps per 4 MB transfer alone, ~39.5 Mbps each with 2 and with 4 at once (155-159 Mbps aggregate), no packets dropped by the relay; 418.7 MB through the relay in total, as in campaigns 1 and 2.

limitations: 3 runs per scenario (4-8 for the parallel relay runs): percentiles over runs are rough; RTT percentiles pool the ~60 latency samples of each run. The lossy-link medians (1.3-28 Mbps per run) say little; its detection rate comes from 13 runs (3 campaign runs + 10 extra in debug/lossy-extra, which are not in summary.json).

The verdict classification is ours (summarize.py), per run by its worst finding; a 'right' run can still have imperfect wording. A packet_loss hint on an unshaped path counts as misleading, also in the real world where one lost packet may be real. A transfer_failed issue is not checked against what the listener received (the one such run is a debug run).
The packet_loss window holds 103-145 packets: at 1 % random loss about one window in three to four shows no loss, so a single run cannot tell 1 % loss from none.

The lab NATs are Linux conntrack + nftables with port preservation, one host per router, silent drops of unsolicited packets and one mapping timeout; the 'inbound packet steals the port' behaviour of the i3D host's NAT is not reproduced, and a NAT reboot keeps the same ports.
One relay per scenario: mapping_varies_by_dest cannot be measured, so hard_nat (two relays) was never exercised; hard_nat_likely (one relay, port not preserved) was.

No rate limits in the lab and fixed transfer sizes (10 MB direct, 4 MB relayed): throughput numbers show slow start for those sizes, not capacity; concurrency throughput on fast paths is quantized by the 200 ms interval tick.
Real world: one location (Helsinki) and one firewall type (ufw); per-flow routes of ~34 or ~37.5 ms between the i3D host and Hetzner shift RTT and throughput by ~8 % between runs and campaigns.

The bench-side request timeout was not exercised (concurrency requests are cut off at 8 s, before the 10 s timeout); the listener timed out the 8 cut-off requests in one extra lossy run and the connection carried on.
The relay load test is bounded (at most 4 parallel 4 MB transfers, ~150 MB through the relay) and does not find the relay's capacity.
--idle cannot show NAT mapping expiry: iroh keeps every path alive every 5 s and the lab's shortest mapping timeout is 5 s.
QUIC loss is counted only for packets the bench node sent; IPv4 only inside the lab.
Runs were sequential, but the i3D host also carries other services; their load was not controlled.
